title: Language core: design patterns in Python
seriesDescription: Singleton, factory, builder, strategy, observer, command, decorators and dependency injection in Python. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Decorators and closures, late binding, Strategy with plain functions, Singleton via modules and __new__, dataclass builders, Observer with callbacks and the usual traps.
source: Gang of Four; Python docs: functools, data model, import system (sys.modules), dataclasses; Fluent Python (Ramalho); Real Python; GeeksforGeeks design pattern interview list

questions.prompt: Write a Python decorator log_calls that prints "calling <function name>" before running the wrapped function, passes all arguments through, returns the result, and keeps the original function metadata.

checks.label: calls and returns the wrapped function

questions.explanation: A decorator is just a callable that takes a function and returns a replacement. A decorator with its own arguments needs one more level of nesting.

questions.prompt: What is the most idiomatic way to implement the Strategy pattern in Python?

options.text: Pass a function or lambda as the strategy argument
options.why: Correct: functions are first-class, so a callable replaces the whole class hierarchy.

options.text: Create an abstract Strategy class with one subclass per algorithm
options.why: Valid but ceremonial; use it when strategies hold state or need several methods.

options.text: Use a metaclass to register algorithms globally
options.why: Overkill and hides the dependency.

options.text: Hard-code an if/elif chain inside the context class
options.why: That is the code smell Strategy removes.

questions.explanation: Examples: sorted(key=...), the key function of max, or a dict mapping names to callables.

questions.prompt:
A developer registers three handlers in Python:
handlers = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
print([h() for h in handlers])
What does it print?

options.why: That would need each lambda to capture its own value at creation time.
Correct: closures capture the variable i, not its value, and the loop leaves i == 2.
range(3) ends at 2, so i never becomes 3.

options.text: NameError: i is not defined
options.why: i is still alive in the enclosing scope after the comprehension via the closure cell.

questions.explanation: Fix with a default argument: lambda i=i: i, or functools.partial. The same late-binding trap hits callbacks registered in loops. (Verified by running it.)

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: Python decorators can only be applied to functions, never to classes.
questions.reason: A decorator is any callable that receives an object and returns a replacement or the same object.

whys.a: A is false, so it cannot be right.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: Correct: class decorators exist (for example @dataclass), so A is false; R correctly defines a decorator.

questions.explanation: @dataclass, @functools.total_ordering and many registries are class decorators.

questions.prompt: In Python, a module-level object is a simple singleton because the interpreter executes a module once and caches it in sys.modules.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: sys.modules makes repeated imports return the same module object, so its top-level objects are created once per process.

options.text: False
options.why: Wrong: the import system caches modules by name, so a second import does not re-run the module body.

questions.explanation: Importing the same module again returns the cached module object, so module-level state is shared. This is why Python code rarely needs a Singleton class; an exception is separate processes or reloading the module.

questions.prompt: Write a Python class Config that behaves as a singleton by overriding __new__, so that Config() always returns the same object.

checks.label: stores the instance on the class
creates it once via super or object

questions.explanation: A module-level instance is simpler and just as good; note that __init__ runs on every Config() call here.

questions.prompt: Write a Python dataclass Pizza with an int field size and a bool field cheese that defaults to False, as the idiomatic replacement for a builder.
questions.explanation: Keyword arguments plus defaults give the readability a builder provides, so Python rarely needs the classic Builder.

questions.prompt: Write a Python class Subject with subscribe(callback) and publish(msg) so that publishing calls every subscribed callback with the message.
questions.explanation: Iterating over a copy lets a callback unsubscribe itself safely while the loop runs.

questions.prompt: Given a list of strings words, write one Python expression that returns a new list sorted by string length, passing the strategy as a function.
questions.explanation: The key argument is the strategy: any function mapping an item to a sort key.

questions.prompt: Select all genuine drawbacks or pitfalls of the Singleton pattern in Python.

options.text: It is hidden global state, which makes tests order-dependent and hard to isolate.
options.why: Tests share the instance unless it is explicitly reset.

options.text: A __new__-based singleton runs __init__ again on every call to the class.
options.why: Python calls __init__ whenever __new__ returns an instance of the class.

options.text: Each worker process in a multi-process server gets its own instance.
options.why: Processes do not share memory, so one "global" is really one per process.

options.text: A module-level instance is created again every time another module imports it.
options.why: Imports are cached in sys.modules, so the module body runs once.

options.text: A singleton can never be created lazily.
options.why: Lazy creation inside __new__ or a function is straightforward.

questions.explanation: Prefer a module-level object or dependency injection; singletons mainly add hidden coupling.

questions.prompt: A class caches one instance in __new__ and its __init__ increments a class counter n (starting at 0) each time it runs. After Config(); Config(); Config(), what is n?
questions.explanation: __new__ returns the same object each time, but Python still calls __init__ on it after every Config() call, so n reaches 3.
